description.narrative: 885 vulnerable IDP HHs (4425 p) in PaP camps and host families in Croix-de-Bouquets

The West department of Haiti, like many regions, grapples with escalating insecurity, exacerbating challenges like internal displacement and food shortages. Between June-August ‘22 over 113,000 ppl were displaced, with 96,000 fleeing the capital due to clashes between gangs and National Police (UN). The violence, alongside poverty and climate change, led to widespread food insecurity, affecting 8.2M ppl by Nov ‘23, with 71.9% of the population in Ouest experiencing it. Economic distress worsened due to inflation. In Dec ‘23, Haiti had 116,952 IDPs, with significant additional displacement during violent attacks in Feb ‘24 (IOM), settling in overcrowded camps in Port-au-Prince (PaP) (57% female, 54% children). According to IOM/GDCP 04/’24,180,837 IDPs live in camps in PaP and 5,620 in host communities in Croix-des-Bouquets (CdB). In Jan ‘24, Cordaid/Christian Aid and partners conducted a Rapid Needs Assessment (RNA), revealing priority needs ranked in order: food, WASH, essential NFI, cash, protection. Next to this RNA, field visits by partner staff to the PaP sites observed the dire living conditions of the IDPs. These contribute to the spread of diseases such as typhoid, diarrheal diseases (cholera, dysentery, etc), and vaginal infections. March ‘24 CCCM Cluster indicated only 25% of WASH and 39% of NFI needs were met across PaP camps. People affected and displaced by conflict urgently need multi-sectoral assistance. CA and partners are already responding in PaP, CdB and N-E, with MPC/WASH/FSL/PSS, but needs are huge. In coordination with other actors, DRA members, with markets still functioning, CA and partners propose to focus this response on MPC and WASH, mainstreaming Protection, to address needs at community and HH level, reducing public health and protection risks. The proposed intervention directly targets 885 HHs in PaP & CdB. Working with local partners embedded in the communities provides readiness to respond quickly, with strong access to communities.

The proposed activities address multisectoral needs and reduce health risks targeting 885 vulnerable IDP HHs (4425 p) in PaP camps and host families in CdB. Through a HH survey and coordination with camp committee & community leaders accurate beneficiary targeting and registration is ensured. Selection criteria prioritize vulnerable HHs, especially those without assistance since Feb 29, 2024. In PaP camps 600HHs will benefit from installation of water tanks, strategically located for easy access, crucial given rising cholera cases and upcoming rainy season. Partnership with local water company ensures water supply. HH will also receive 2 jerrycans. The 600HHs in PaP and 285HH in CdB receive 2 rounds of hygiene kits to be collected at local suppliers minimizing transport/safety risks. This comprehensive approach promotes hygiene, reduces disease transmission risks (e.g., cholera). Out of these HHs, 358HHs most vulnerable will be targeted with 2 rounds of MPC, to meet most urgent needs, providing choice and dignity: 255 HH in camps in PaP (MEB for NFI, complementing WFP food); 103 HHs in host communities in CdB (full MEB). Amounts are harmonised with CashWG. Protection will be mainstreamed. Awareness sessions will focus on people’s rights regarding assistance, GBV risks, acquiring skills and strategies to protect themselves/family members. Partners’ social workers will ensure IDP awareness on protection and provide PFA to those who need it, like GBV survivors. Individuals with additional (protection) needs will receive appropriate referrals to other JR members like WV or other actors. In coordination with the protection cluster and IBESR, particular attention will be paid to children in need of protection (like orphans). CA coordinated with WV and StC to avoid duplication, and will continue to work closely with other JR members/actors to avoid duplication and seek complementarity, and collaborate with the CVWG, IOM, Civil Protection, FS/WASH Clusters, and OCHA.

title.narrative: CSH-R1: Number of people benefitting from unconditional and unrestricted cash transfers

description.narrative: Unconditional transfers are provided to beneficiaries without the recipient having to do anything in return in order to receive the assistance . Unrestricted transfers can be used entirely as the recipient chooses i.e. there are no restrictions on how the transfer is spent (Definitions of CALP). It can be delivered e.g. through local banks, shops, traders, local money transfer companies, remittance companies and post offices in either one or several instalments.

title.narrative: WSH-R4: Number of people having access to sufficient and safe water for domestic use

description.narrative: Access: maximum distance to water point 500m, queuing time less than 15min, filling time maximum 3 min/20 litres or as locally agreed. Water access should be during the whole period of implementation unless action is mostly related to building the local water delivery capacity. Sufficient: covering basic needs, i.e. 7.5-15 l/p/d or as locally agreed. Safe: 1) low risk of faecal contamination, 2) No faecal coliforms detectable in any 100-ml sample, 3) For piped water supplies, or for all water supplies at times of risk or presence of diarrhoea epidemic, water is treated with a disinfectant to achieve free chlorine residual at the tap of 0.5 mg per litre and turbidity is below 5 NTU, 4) If for a short period, water which is contaminated chemically or radiologically is used, no (significant probability of) negative health effect is (likely to be) detected. Domestic use: drinking, cooking and personal hygiene (incl. laundry)

title.narrative: ACC-R1: Number of crisis-affected people who are also involved in the design, implementation, monitoring and/or evaluation of the programme

description.narrative: Participation is defined as the involvement of crisis-affected people in one or more phases of the programme: assessment, design, implementation, monitoring or evaluation. Participation does not take place when activities are carried out in exchange for a salary of 'in-kind' payment unless the affected people are involved in decision-making processes and have an impact on decisions that affect them. Please describe in the activity description what this involvement specifically entails and in which phase of the program conflict-affected people are involved.

title.narrative: WSH-R6: Number of people reached with hygiene promotion/awareness raising activities

description.narrative: Hygiene promotion/awareness raising activities. Could be training, campaigns, radio broadcasts, flyers etc. Excludes the distribution of Hygiene/dignity kits that should be covered under WHS-I1.

title.narrative: WSH-R1: Number of people having regular access to soap to meet hygienic needs

description.narrative: Regular and timely access: 250g soap/p/m for personal hygiene, 200g soap/p/month for laundry. This includes hygiene/dignity kits. Access may be in-kind or though voucher distribution or through unconditional restricted cash to enable beneficiary to buy soap (without compromising access to other basic needs). Distributed items need to be culturally acceptable i.e. take into account local practice and expectations.

title.narrative: LOC-R2: % of budget spent on capacity building of national an local actors

description.narrative: This concerns capacity building such as training and on the job support to national and local actors. This is captured under "Capacity building local partners" in the DRA budget. Note that this does not include local offices of INGOs.

title.narrative: LOC-R3: Number of national and local actors supported with capacity-building

description.narrative: Total number of national and local actors that received capacity-building support during implementation. In case more than one individual from a national/local actor participates in the capacity building activities, this counts as one national/local actor. Note that this does not include local offices of INGOs.
